## Read this first

A plan is read once, under pressure, by somebody who did not write it. So every
step below names a real thing — an endpoint, an alert, a script — and **the
generator refuses to render if any of them does not exist**. Routes are checked
against the live router, alerts against the rules the chart ships, files against
the repository. A renamed route breaks the build rather than the response.

Steps marked with the placeholder are decisions or actions only a person can
take. They are in the plan because leaving them out would imply the software
handles them; they are blank because a plan naming a fictional on-call rota is
worse than no plan, since somebody will follow it.

**Every containment lever is reversible except C6.** That is deliberate and it
is the most useful thing on this page: you can act early without deciding
anything permanent.

Eleven blank fields, and the plan is not usable until they are filled in. That is
the honest state of LG-8: the levers exist and are proven, the sequence is
written down, and the organisation around it does not exist yet.

## 1. Detect

How you find out. Nothing here phones home, so every signal is one the customer owns.

### D1 — Check the alerts.

**Use:** `IgniAuditWriteFailing`  `IgniDependencyDown`  `IgniServerErrors`  `IgniClockSkew` · `charts/igni/files/alerts.yaml`

**Proven by:** `LG-7` (Verified)

The rules ship with the chart, each carrying a description that says what to do — a count is not quoted here because it was wrong within a pass of being written elsewhere. IgniAuditWriteFailing fires on a single occurrence, because one lost audit record is worth knowing about; IgniClockSkew fires when a replica drifts far enough that a session withdrawal can be outlived.

### D2 — Read the audit trail, filtered to denials.

**Use:** `GET /v1/portal/audit-events`

**Proven by:** `LG-1` (Verified), `LG-3` (Verified), `LG-4` (Verified)

Every authentication attempt is recorded including failures, and a denied privileged action is the row this trail exists for. Filterable by actor, target and outcome.

### D3 — Check whether backups are still being taken.

**Use:** `containers/backup.sh`

**Proven by:** `DP-11` (Verified)

`.last-success` in the backup directory is written only after an archive has been verified, so its age is the honest signal. The compose healthcheck goes red at two intervals; a stale marker during an incident means the recovery option in phase 6 may not exist.

### D4 — Somebody told you.

**A decision, not a mechanism.** `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__`

## 2. Triage

Decide what it is and how bad, before touching anything.

### T1 — Write down what you know, with timestamps, before changing anything.

**A decision, not a mechanism.** `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__`

Containment destroys evidence — a withdrawn session stops the requests you would have wanted to see. Five minutes of notes first is the difference between a scope you can state and one you have to guess.

### T2 — Classify it.

**A decision, not a mechanism.** `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__`

### T3 — Establish whether personal data is involved, because that starts a clock.

**Use:** `POST /v1/portal/subject-access` · `docs/RECORDS_OF_PROCESSING.md`

**Proven by:** `DP-8` (Verified), `DP-9` (Verified)

The subject-access report is the fastest way to see what the deployment holds about a person; the records of processing say which tables could be in scope at all.

## 3. Contain

Stop it continuing. Every lever here is reversible except the last.

### C1 — Withdraw one person's sessions.

**Use:** `POST /v1/portal/team/{user_id}/revoke-sessions`  `POST /v1/portal/me/revoke-sessions`

**Proven by:** `AC-11` (Verified)

Every token that person holds stops working on the next request — portal, CLI and desktop app. Reversible: they sign in again and get a new one. This is the lever for a suspected leaked credential and it does not require deleting anybody.

### C2 — Deactivate their membership.

**Use:** `PATCH /v1/portal/team/{user_id}/status`

**Proven by:** `AC-11` (Verified), `AC-3` (Verified)

Cuts organisation access on the next request, and is reversible. Different from C1 and both are usually right: deactivation stops them reaching this organisation, withdrawal stops the credential itself.

### C3 — Rotate the encryption key.

**Use:** `tools/rotate_secret_key.py`

**Proven by:** `DP-2` (Verified)

Both keys live during the change: the new one encrypts, the previous one still decrypts, and the tool re-encrypts stored rows — reporting what it would do before it writes. Do this when the key itself may have been exposed, not for a leaked user credential.

### C4 — Take a GPU node out of rotation.

**Use:** `POST /v1/portal/inference/nodes/{node_id}/drain`

**Proven by:** `AV-1` (Verified)

Drains it without deleting it, and the drain survives the cluster re-announcing itself — registration is idempotent and would otherwise overwrite the change within 180 seconds. Only Resume clears it.

### C5 — Rotate the shared secrets an attacker may hold.

**Use:** `docs/self-hosting.md`

**Proven by:** `CM-5` (Verified)

The node registration token and the super-admin key are separate values on purpose: the node token lives in Terraform and cloud-init, a much wider blast radius than the other, and each must be rotatable without taking the other down. Configuration change plus a restart; the startup checks refuse anything too short. No secret is shared with a service such as Artifacts or CodeIndex: one whose own key may be compromised is revoked on the portal's Services page, which stops its tokens at once, and approved again after it registers a new key.

### C6 — Delete the account.

**Use:** `DELETE /v1/portal/team/{user_id}`

**Proven by:** `AC-11` (Verified), `DP-7` (Verified)

The last resort, and the only irreversible one here. It ends every session the account issued and is swept across the whole authenticated surface. Prefer C1 and C2 while you still need the person's history to be attributable.

## 4. Investigate

Establish scope from records that cannot have been altered.

### I1 — Export the audit trail as JSON Lines and work on the copy.

**Use:** `GET /v1/portal/audit-events/export`

**Proven by:** `LG-2` (Verified), `LG-4` (Verified)

The table is append-only — `UPDATE` is refused by a database trigger, and the refusal survives a restore — so the original cannot be tidied up by accident. The export is itself audited, because it hands somebody the whole trail.

### I2 — Establish who had access, and when they last used it.

**Use:** `GET /v1/portal/access-review`

**Proven by:** `AC-8` (Verified)

Members, roles and last sign-in. Answers "was this account dormant" without a database query.

### I3 — Establish what the deployment holds about an affected person.

**Use:** `POST /v1/portal/subject-access`

**Proven by:** `DP-8` (Verified)

Every classified personal-data column, from the same classification the build asserts against the live schema — so the report cannot silently omit a column a migration added.

### I4 — Check the clocks before trusting the ordering.

**Use:** `IgniClockSkew`

**Proven by:** `LG-7` (Verified)

The trail is read newest-first with keyset pagination on `occurred_at`, which is an app clock. Skew between replicas mis-orders it and can skip a row at a page boundary — so a timeline assembled during an incident is only as good as `igni_clock_skew_seconds` says it is.

## 5. Notify

Obligations with clocks on them.

### N1 — Decide whether this is a personal-data breach, and record the reasoning.

**A decision, not a mechanism.** `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__`

### N2 — If it is, notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware.

**A decision, not a mechanism.** `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__`

### N3 — Consider whether affected people must be told directly.

**A decision, not a mechanism.** `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__`

### N4 — Tell the customer, if this deployment is not yours.

**A decision, not a mechanism.** `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__`

### N5 — Be ready for the requests that follow a notification.

**Use:** `POST /v1/portal/subject-access`  `POST /v1/portal/erasure`

**Proven by:** `DP-8` (Verified), `DP-7` (Verified)

People told their data was involved exercise their rights, and both routes exist: a subject-access report covering every classified column, and erasure that redacts a named person from their documents without destroying other people's comments on them.

## 6. Recover

Return to a known-good state.

### R1 — Restore from a verified backup if data was destroyed or altered.

**Use:** `tools/restore-drill.sh`  `containers/backup.sh`

**Proven by:** `DP-10` (Verified), `DP-11` (Verified)

The drill that runs in CI is the procedure: restore, compare schema and rows, check the encrypted credentials byte for byte, confirm the append-only trigger survived, and boot the application against the restored database before believing it.

### R2 — Re-issue what you revoked.

**Use:** `PATCH /v1/portal/team/{user_id}/status`  `POST /v1/portal/inference/nodes/{node_id}/drain`

**Proven by:** `AC-11` (Verified), `AV-1` (Verified)

Reactivate memberships, reconnect integrations, resume drained nodes. Everything in phase 3 except C6 is reversible, which is why C6 is last.

### R3 — Confirm the deployment is actually healthy, not merely running.

**Use:** `GET /ready`

**Proven by:** `AV-1` (Verified)

`/ready` distinguishes liveness from readiness and names each dependency, so a green process with a dead database is visible rather than reassuring.

## 7. Learn

The step that is always skipped.

### L1 — Write down what happened, what it cost, and the rule that keeps it fixed.

**Use:** `docs/REVIEW_FINDINGS.md`

The pre-production review applied that practice to defects, finding by finding (indexed in `docs/REVIEW_FINDINGS.md`). The shape transfers: a fix without a rule is a fix that comes back, and the rule is what makes the write-up worth the hour.

### L2 — Add the check that would have caught it.

**Use:** `docs/POLICIES.md`

**Proven by:** `CM-1` (Verified)

The recurring lesson of this codebase: a guard over the live router, the live schema or the shipped artefact, rather than a corrected call site. A list of call sites rots.

### L3 — Update the risk assessment.

**Use:** `docs/RISK_ASSESSMENT.md`

It is built from realised risks, so a new incident belongs in it as observed rather than estimated. If the incident is a new risk, add it; if it is an old one, its treatment was insufficient and that is the finding.

### L4 — Review whether this plan helped.

**A decision, not a mechanism.** `__ORGANISATION_TO_COMPLETE__`

## What this plan is honest about

**It has never been rehearsed.** Every lever in phase 3 is individually tested —
there are tests that a withdrawn session is refused on every authenticated route,
that a drain survives re-registration, that a rotation keeps both keys live, and
that a restore comes back byte for byte. Nobody has run them in sequence against
a deployment while pretending to be under attack. A tabletop exercise is the
cheapest next thing and it is the organisation's to schedule.

**Containment destroys evidence.** T1 exists because of it: withdrawing a session
stops the requests you would have wanted to see. The order here puts five minutes
of note-taking before the first lever, which is the opposite of the instinct.

**Nothing here phones home.** No vendor is watching this deployment and none can
help unless asked — every signal in phase 1 is one the customer runs. That is the
point of the product and it is also a responsibility that comes with it.

**The 72-hour clock starts at awareness, not at breach.** Which means phase 2
is on the clock too, and T1's timestamps are what establish when awareness
began.
